newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-SUPER LEAGUE STRUGGLES TO CONVINCE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-SUPER LEAGUE STRUGGLES TO CONVINCE.

text.p: Super League, the breakaway rugby league competition owned by media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, faces a battle to win over Australian fans following modest crowd figures at the opening round of matches.

Despite giving away a generous but undisclosed number of free tickets, attendances fell well below those recorded in the early 1990s, before Murdoch's bid to claim rugby league as a promotional tool for his various pay television interests.
News Limited, the Australian arm of Murdoch's media empire, has invested several hundred million dollars in the 10-team Super League, poaching several existing clubs and a host of top players.
But the promise to create the world's best rugby league competition fell a little flat on Saturday when Brisbane beat Auckland in an opening fixture of poor quality.

The inferior standard of play prompted even the Murdoch-owned Sydney Daily Telegraph newspaper to comment: "Super League promised the best of the best but the Saturday night game was bumbling at best with more than 40 errors".
Super League added to their huge investment by spending an estimated A$600,000 ($468,000) on pre-match entertainment at the five grounds hosting the opening round of matches.
Some of that money paid for two brief performances by American pop singer Belinda Carlisle, who was flown in from the United States to add a little glamour to the occasion.

Despite the massive expenditure to lure fans, supported by a advertising campaign on television and radio over recent weeks, the Sydney Football Stadium attendance for Cronulla's 26-4 victory over Canberra on Monday was 22,653, leaving the ground half-empty.
"We are out to make the game better and that will happen," News Ltd executive chairman Ken Cowley told The Australian newspaper on Monday.

"I would describe it as a modestly good start for Super League this weekend," said Cowley, whose company has budgeted to spend an estimated A$6.0 million ($4.68 million) on pre-match and half-time entertainment during the season.
In addition to the widespread criticism over the standard of play in several matches, there were also grumbles about the glitzy presentation, which included firework displays and cheer squads.

"We didn't come to see all this hoopla, we came to see the football. This is never going to work," Penrith supporter Mick Hoolihan told The Sydney Morning Herald, the only daily metropolitan paper in the city not controlled by Murdoch.
The rival Australian Rugby League (ARL) 12-team premiership will kick off its 1997 season next weekend, pitching the two organisations into direct competition.
Murdoch divided the sport when he lured several clubs, including former champions Brisbane, Canberra and Sydney Bulldogs, to defect from the ARL premiership.
Brisbane, traditionally the best supported rugby league team in Australia, attracted 40,000, the biggest crowd of the weekend, to watch their clash with Auckland.
But fewer than 7,000 fans saw the newly-created franchise Hunter Mariners lose at home to Sydney Bulldogs in Newcastle, while 8,000 Penrith followers watched their team beat Perth on Sunday.
